Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

vignette: Luis, a 22-year-old Latin American male and product manager, has been struggling with symptoms of post-traumatic stress following his experiences in a war-torn region where he was caught up in intense fighting. Luis had come to the United States for work but found himself in the crossfire during a routine trip back home to visit family. The traumatic event occurred one evening when he and his cousin were walking through their neighborhood, which suddenly came under gunfire from an unknown group of combatants. Luis managed to flee but not before witnessing several casualties and narrowly escaping injury himself. In the weeks following this harrowing experience, Luis found that his body remained perpetually tense, as if always ready for the next attack. He was superalert or watchful, constantly scanning his environment for any sign of danger. This hypervigilance extended into his daily life in America; he would often jump at unexpected movements nearby, reacting as if they were imminent threats. The fear and overwhelming feelings that Luis experienced led him to engage in maladaptive strategies such as self-harm. He had come to believe that hurting himself physically was the only way to release the intense emotions he felt. This behavior began shortly after his return, with Luis finding small ways to inflict pain on himself during moments of high anxiety. Seeking reassurance became another coping mechanism for Luis. He frequently asked colleagues and friends if they thought he was okay or if there were any signs that something bad might happen again. The constant need for validation made him appear needy and clingy, straining his relationships at work and in social settings. Luis also developed the habit of constantly checking his body for signs of danger or injury. He would feel his limbs and torso repeatedly throughout the day to ensure he wasn't injured. This behavior was a way for Luis to maintain control over his perceived vulnerability but often led him to miss important details during meetings, causing frustration among his colleagues. Over time, these symptoms began to take a toll on his professional life as a product manager. His hypervigilance and need for reassurance made it difficult for him to focus on his tasks effectively. Meetings that required quick decision-making were particularly challenging because Luis was often preoccupied with the possibility of threats rather than concentrating on business strategies. The culmination of these struggles pushed Luis to seek help. Recently, he had an incident at work where a sudden movement from a colleague startled him so severely that he nearly left his desk in panic. This episode made it clear to Luis that his symptoms were not only affecting his mental health but also threatening his career and personal relationships. What frightened Luis most was the fear of losing control and being unable to function normally, both at work and in his daily life. He was certain that these intrusive thoughts and behaviors would continue unless he found a way to manage them effectively. Luis expressed hope that with professional help, he could regain some sense of normalcy and feel safe again. Luis's current state reflects a deep-seated fear and an intense need for relief from the overwhelming emotions and physical reactions he experiences daily. He hopes therapy will provide him with tools to mitigate his symptoms and allow him to live without constantly feeling on guard or in danger.
